column4: The section makes the womb a house where the child is formed; this ayah says Allah shapes people in the wombs (ٱلْأَرْحَامِ), making that hidden home an act of divine formation.
The section calls the womb a child's house and vessel; this ayah places creation within three layers of darkness in the womb, giving that shelter a concrete bodily setting.
The section describes a child being brought along toward completion; this ayah moves from drop to formed and unformed lump, then birth and maturity, making growth in stages explicit.
The section begins with the womb as the child's place of origin; this ayah traces human creation from an extract of clay toward the later stages of gestation.
The section calls the womb a house and vessel; this ayah places the drop in a secure resting-place (قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ), directly extending the image of protected lodging.
The section's dictionary gloss defines tarbiya as taking something state by state to completion; this ayah names successive bodily transformations and then a further creation.
The section describes growth from one state to another until completion; this ayah traces creation through drop, clot, infant, maturity, and old age.
The section presents the womb as a house for the growing child; this ayah calls the embryo's place a secure repository (قَرَارٍ مَكِينٍ), giving the shelter image a direct parallel.
The section's upbringing proceeds toward completion over time; this ayah says the embryo remains there until a known term (قَدَرٍ مَعْلُومٍ).
The section says care carries a thing through stages to its limit; this ayah names divine measuring and determining in the embryo's development.

The section says the womb is where Allah shapes a child as He wills; this ayah says Allah knows what every female carries and what wombs diminish or increase, placing development under measured knowledge.
The section frames the womb as the first home before a child's later upbringing; this ayah says people are brought out of their mothers' wombs knowing nothing, then given hearing, sight, and hearts.
The section follows the child from the womb into a family that cares for it; this ayah moves from pregnancy to birth and the parents' prayer for a sound child.
The section treats the womb as a child's home; Mary's mother dedicates what is in her womb, making the unborn child the center of a household vow.
The section moves from womb to the child's later life; this ayah records Mary's birth and her mother's naming her, carrying the image from gestation into family care.
The section says a child can be raised by someone other than the one who gave birth; this ayah says Zakariyya took charge of Mary (كَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا) and that she grew under his care.
The section makes the womb and later upbringing one continuum; this ayah names a mother's strain in carrying and weaning her child, then commands gratitude to parents.
The section links womb, birth, and raising a child; this ayah names the mother's hardship in pregnancy and delivery, the full gestation-and-weaning term, and a prayer for righteous descendants.

The section moves from the womb into nurture at home; this ayah sets nursing and weaning, forbids harming either parent through the child, and assigns the child's father provision and clothing for the nursing mother.
The section follows the child from the womb into a life outside it; this ayah says Mary conceived and withdrew with him, giving a concrete mother-and-child scene.
The section's dictionary note describes a mother animal suffering in her womb after giving birth; this ayah gives the human parallel of Mary's labor pain, specifically linking birth to bodily cost.
The section presents care as meeting a vulnerable mother and child; in the immediate birth scene this ayah answers Mary's distress with reassurance and a stream beneath her.
The section's house image includes provision for a growing child; this ayah tells Mary to shake the palm trunk so fresh dates fall for her after labor.
The section joins maternal care with the child's home; this ayah tells Mary to eat, drink, and be comforted after delivery.
The section brings the word Rabb into a family setting; this ayah begins the command to worship Allah alone and show ihsan to one's parents.

The section's roots are joined in this prayer: the source's dictionary form raḥmah appears in ٱرْحَمْهُمَا, and its child-rearing sense of rabb appears in رَبَّيَانِي; grown children ask care for the parents who raised them.
The section says kin are named through the womb because they came from one womb; this ayah joins reverence for Allah with care for ٱلْأَرْحَامِ, making the bodily origin a social bond.
The section explains kinship through people emerging from one womb; this ayah says blood relatives are closer to one another in Allah's Book, giving that tie a practical priority.
The section's listed dictionary form rabība means a girl cared for by a step-parent; this ayah names الرَّبَائِبُ and locates them in the household's حجر, the very family setting the image develops.

The section defines upbringing as carrying someone to completion; this ayah orders guardians to test orphans until they reach marriageable maturity and then return their property, specifying care up to adulthood.
The section presents a household that shelters and raises a child; this ayah protects the treasure of two orphan boys until they reach strength, explaining the shelter through their righteous father.
The section uses Moses' infancy to show care continuing after birth; this ayah commands his mother to nurse him and, when afraid, place him in the river.
The section's child leaves his mother's home and is taken into another household; this ayah says Pharaoh's people picked Moses up, setting the foster-household scene in motion.
The section describes another household's care for Moses; Pharaoh's wife calls him an eye's delight for herself and her husband and asks that he not be killed.
The section names the separation between mother and child; this ayah says Moses' mother's heart became empty, showing the cost of the child's removal.
The section follows a family trying to protect a child from afar; this ayah says Moses' sister watched him from a distance while they did not recognize her.
The section's dictionary form rāb/rābba means a spouse who takes up a child's upbringing; this ayah offers Pharaoh's household a family who will nurse and care for Moses.
The section says the child returns from another household to his mother; this ayah says Allah returned Moses to her so her eye would be comforted.
The section defines tarbiya as carrying something state by state to completion; this ayah marks Moses reaching maturity and receiving judgment and knowledge.
The section uses Moses' infancy to show divine care working through his mother; this ayah recalls Allah inspiring Moses' mother before the rescue by the river.
The section says the child is raised under the Lord's care; this ayah recounts placing Moses in the chest and says he was brought up under Allah's eye (عَلَىٰ عَيْنِي).
The section follows Moses through separation, reunion, and growth; this ayah recalls his sister's intervention, his return to his mother, and his reaching maturity.
The section calls Pharaoh's upbringing claim incomplete; Pharaoh says he raised Moses among his household as a child, giving the claim the exact words the section qualifies.
After Pharaoh's upbringing claim in 26:18, this ayah supplies his accusation against Moses; it shows the palace's account of care is immediately framed as a grievance and charge of ingratitude.
The section explicitly links its dictionary sense of rabb as a teacher who feeds people small units of knowledge to rabbāniyyūn; this ayah says to be rabbāniyyūn through teaching the Book.
The section develops Rahman as a teacher; this ayah names ٱلرَّحْمَٰنِ, whose teaching of the Qur'an is stated in 55:2.
The section says a teacher feeds learners small portions of knowledge; this ayah gives the Rahman the direct act عَلَّمَ ٱلْقُرْءَانَ, teaching the Qur'an.
The section joins nurture and creation in the image of a child growing; this ayah places creation of the human between the Rahman's teaching of Qur'an and teaching of expression.
The section's teacher develops the learner's capacities; this ayah says the human was taught البيان, the ability to express and make clear.
The section's dictionary gloss calls the learned teacher one who feeds people small sciences; this ayah shows Allah teaching Adam the names, a foundational act of instruction.
The section extends upbringing into teaching; Abraham asks for a messenger who will recite signs and teach the Book and wisdom to his descendants.
The section makes teaching part of nurture; this ayah says the Messenger recites, purifies, and teaches the Book and wisdom to the believers.
The section's image extends care into instruction; this ayah repeats the sequence of recitation, purification, and teaching the Book and wisdom.
The section describes development state by state; this ayah explains that the Qur'an came in stages to strengthen the Prophet's heart and be recited distinctly.
The section's teacher nourishes learners through small portions; this ayah says the Qur'an was divided so it could be recited to people over intervals.
The section's teacher develops learners gradually; this ayah tells the Prophet not to hasten ahead of revelation and to ask, رَبِّ زِدْنِي عِلْمًا, for increased knowledge.
The section describes the teacher who nourishes people with small sciences; this ayah says the Lord taught by the pen, giving learning a concrete means.
The section describes bringing a learner from one state toward completion; this ayah says Allah taught the human what he did not know.
The section's dictionary form qiwām describes what keeps a household standing; this ayah calls wealth قِيَامًا لِّلنَّاسِ and immediately orders provision and clothing for dependents.
The section links al-mustaqīm's root q-w-m to qiwām, the one who sustains a household; this ayah calls men قَوَّامُونَ over women and connects that role to spending from their wealth.
The section's dictionary note gives a secondary sense of ghayra as provisions brought home; the brothers say نَمِيرُ أَهْلَنَا, that they will procure provisions for their family.
The section says a household's affairs are kept standing by its sustainer; this ayah commands the Prophet to enjoin prayer on his family and says, نَحْنُ نَرْزُقُكَ, that Allah provides.
The section moves from womb to home care; this ayah orders housing for divorced mothers, spending during pregnancy, and payment or consultation over nursing the child.
The section's secondary gloss of ghayra evokes protecting one's household; this ayah directly commands believers to protect themselves and their families from the Fire.
The section's dictionary gloss describes a newly delivered ewe kept at home for milk; this ayah describes milk produced by livestock, a concrete parallel to the household's animal nourishment.
The section's dictionary gloss makes milk from a lactating ewe part of household provision; this ayah points to livestock as a source of drink and food.
The section's womb-and-house image includes feeding and sheltering a child; Abraham leaves some descendants in a barren valley and asks Allah to provide fruit for them and turn hearts toward them.
The section describes family care that helps a child grow toward completion; this prayer asks for spouses and offspring who are a comfort to the eyes and for the family to lead the mindful.
The section's home carries a duty to feed and protect the child; this ayah forbids killing children from poverty and says Allah provides for both parents and children.
The section presents care as protection and provision for the vulnerable child; this ayah forbids killing children for poverty and says Allah provides for them and their parents.
The section defines raḥmah as tenderness that leads to good treatment; this ayah places affection and mercy between spouses, locating that care within a household.
The section says mercy becomes ihsan, especially toward the weak; this ayah commands justice and ihsan and names giving to close kin.
The section describes mercy as practical goodness toward relatives and the weak; this ayah commands ihsan to parents, kin, orphans, and the needy.
The section makes care for family and the vulnerable an expression of goodness; this ayah names parents, near relatives, orphans, and the needy as recipients of spending.
The section says kinship grows from a shared womb and calls for care; this ayah commands giving close relatives their due, along with the needy and traveler.
The section's home shelters a child who depends on another's care; this ayah says Allah found the Prophet an orphan and gave him shelter.
The section's image joins care with provision; this ayah says Allah found the Prophet in need and made him self-sufficient.
The section says mercy is directed especially to the weak; this ayah turns the Prophet's experience of orphanhood into the command not to oppress an orphan.
The section defines mercy as tenderness that becomes good action; this ayah commands not to repel the one who asks.
The section defines mercy as active good toward the vulnerable; this ayah condemns the denier of judgment, whose conduct is specified in the following verses.
The section calls for care of the weak; this ayah describes the opposite conduct, harshly repelling the orphan.
The section says mercy becomes concrete help; this ayah condemns failing to urge food for the needy.
The section says mercy is tenderness that becomes help for the weak; this ayah names feeding on a day of hunger as a hard moral passage.
The section links a shared womb to kinship and care; this ayah names an orphan who is a near relative as a recipient of food.
The section directs tenderness toward the vulnerable; this ayah names a needy person in severe hardship as a recipient of food.
The section's root raḥmah means tenderness that leads to good; this ayah calls believers to urge one another to patience and mercy (مَرْحَمَة).
The section defines raḥmah as doing good to the one shown mercy, especially the weak; this ayah depicts feeding the needy, orphan, and captive out of love for Allah.
The section joins mercy with kinship care; this ayah tells those with means not to withhold from relatives and the poor, but to pardon and overlook.
The section defines raḥmah as a tenderness that leads to good treatment; this ayah says the Prophet was gentle with people by Allah's mercy.
The section makes mercy a response to another's hardship; this ayah says the Messenger is distressed by believers' suffering and is compassionate and merciful toward them.
The section extends tenderness into a bond between people; this ayah describes the believers as merciful toward one another (رُحَمَاءُ بَيْنَهُمْ).
The section says Allah shapes the child in the womb as He wills; this ayah says Allah gives daughters or sons as He wills, placing a child's sex within divine choice.
The section's womb image is a home for a child being formed; this ayah supplies the boundary case of barrenness, where no child is granted.
The section explains kinship through the womb; this ayah names cutting the womb-ties (تُقَطِّعُوا أَرْحَامَكُمْ) as the opposite of honoring that bond.
After 47:22 names cutting womb-ties, this ayah gives the consequence of that rupture: divine curse and loss of sight and hearing.
The section presents kinship as a bond issuing from one womb; this ayah condemns breaking the covenant and the ties Allah commanded to be joined.
The section distinguishes the womb from later care by another adult; this ayah sets the boundary that a man's wife does not become his mother by speech, and says mothers are those who gave birth.
The section includes step-parents who raise a child; this ayah distinguishes adopted sons from biological sons, clarifying that care and lineage are related but not identical.
The section allows a child to be raised by someone other than a birth parent; this ayah says adopted children should be called by their fathers when known, preserving lineage within that care.
The section's dictionary note includes children raised in comfort; this ayah questions whether wealth and children are being mistaken for good things hurried by Allah.
The section notes the luxury sense in raising children; this ayah completes the warning that wealth and children do not prove that Allah is hastening good for their owners.
